_comment: Digest of the migration chain reviewed for outbound behaviour. Re-pin only after reviewing the diff.

reviews.units: U2 slice B1 (#647) — the retain-and-scrub erasure ledger, inert and unreachable

outbound_sweep.method: every sanitizer sweep pattern applied to the one added migration: cron.schedule, cron.alter_job, net.http_post, net.http_request_queue, supabase_functions.http_request, extensions.http_, dblink, CREATE FOREIGN TABLE/SERVER, schedule_in_database, vault.*, CREATE EXTENSION, pg_read_, COPY
outbound_sweep.migrations_with_outbound_capability: none — every pattern returned zero matches, including inside comments and string literals. The sweep was re-run against the final migration text after the ABC-14 access changes and after the round-1 and round-2 review corrections, and returned zero matches each time.
outbound_sweep.new_outbound_capable_functions: none. The migration defines two functions: a plpgsql BEFORE-row trigger guard, and a CREATE OR REPLACE of the existing IMMUTABLE SECURITY DEFINER backup_export_tables() whose body is a VALUES literal. Neither reaches net.http_post, supabase_functions.http_request, dblink or extensions.http_*, so reviewed-outbound-functions.tsv is unchanged
outbound_sweep.new_extensions: none — no CREATE EXTENSION, so reviewed-extensions.tsv is unchanged
outbound_sweep.new_cron_jobs: none — no cron.schedule or cron.alter_job, so reviewed-cron-jobs.tsv is unchanged
outbound_sweep.false_positives_checked: none to check; the sweep produced no hits at all

why_the_sanitized_clone_stays_outbound_i: There is nothing to neutralise. The migration is one CREATE TABLE, three CREATE INDEX, one trigger function, two CREATE TRIGGER, an RLS enable, one REVOKE, a CREATE OR REPLACE of backup_export_tables(), and comments. It touches no scheduler, no network primitive, no extension and no foreign data wrapper, so a sanitized rehearsal target replays it exactly as production would.

The one SECURITY DEFINER object is a redefinition of an already-reviewed function. Its body is a static VALUES list of table names; it takes no argument, reads no table, and runs SET search_path = pg_catalog, public, pg_temp. CREATE OR REPLACE preserves the REVOKE/GRANT set installed by 20261118100000, and scripts/db/backup-coverage.mjs re-asserts on every run that anon and authenticated cannot execute it and service_role can.

The new table is created EMPTY, has NO authorized caller, and grants no privilege to any client role — anon, authenticated and service_role are all revoked and there are zero RLS policies. Nothing in this release writes to it, and nothing can. The migration also does not read, update or delete a row in any existing table.

account_deletion_audit is untouched. Every occurrence of that name in the migration is inside a comment; src/test/u2AccountScrubOperations.pglite.test.ts snapshots that table's rows AND its columns, constraints, triggers, guard body and indexes across the migration and asserts both are byte-identical.
review_history: The first draft added a protocol-2 lane to account_deletion_audit. It was replaced, not patched, after an independent read-only audit reproduced two permanent-wedge defects: a caller-supplied future started_at, and a worker clock ahead of Postgres writing a future auth_deleted_at. Both left an operation with no legal exit while the one-active-operation index blocked any replacement — an account that could not be erased. Closed by the database owning every timestamp and by deleting every cross-timestamp CHECK; ordering is now structural via the transition graph. Both variants are pinned by regression tests.

ABC-14 (owner-approved) then removed the direct service_role grant and the admin SELECT policy. The policy could never have fired — authenticated holds no SELECT privilege — and the grant would have let any holder of the service key write any transition on any row, which the guard trigger cannot prevent because it validates transition shape, not caller entitlement. Access will arrive as narrow SECURITY DEFINER RPCs; none is in B1.

Sixteen guards were mutation-checked: each removed in isolation, then the invariant it claims to enforce probed. All sixteen failed without their guard. Three needed sharper probes first: two (the append-only DELETE refusal and the subject_person_id bind-once exemption) are ALSO caught by a second guard, so the probes assert the specific refusal reason rather than merely that an error occurred; and the ACL probe was initially unfalsifiable because bare Postgres grants nothing by default — the harness now models Supabase's standing ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES, under which deleting the REVOKE does restore privileges to all three roles.

Verified against real Postgres, not only PGlite: after supabase db reset the table's relacl is {postgres=arwdDxtm/postgres} with RLS on and zero policies. Getting there required adding the table to the deny-list in supabase/seed.sql, whose local-only blanket GRANT ALL TO service_role had been silently re-granting everything the migration revoked — so local and CI would have tested the opposite of production.

Codex gpt-5.6-sol/ultra reviewed the first committed head (9f8293316) in thread 019ff061-9be2-7ef3-b0ee-720df894d26b: no P1/P2, five P3, all five confirmed and fixed. The material one was a CHECK NULL escape hatch — `last_error_code IN (...)` without a preceding IS NOT NULL evaluates to NULL and a CHECK accepts NULL, so a terminal failure or a backing-off retry could carry no reason at all. Also fixed: the zero-attempt arm now requires both external markers null; external_attempt_count widened to bigint, which does not abolish the overflow ceiling but moves it from 2^31 to 2^63 — on the order of 10^13 years at the five-minute lease floor, i.e. out of physical reach rather than merely far away; backup-coverage.mjs now asserts the default-deny set BY NAME (the derived sweep passed trivially if a table stopped being closed); the ACL matrix gained TRIGGER; and the stale-lease test was rewritten so it cannot be read as fencing coverage — it now also asserts that WITHOUT the predicate the write succeeds, which is the honest state until the RPCs land. That review cleared no head: it predates these corrections and the owner's wording audit.

Codex round 2 reviewed abb25f850 in the same thread: again no P1/P2, six P3. Five were classified as introduced by or incomplete round-1 fixes and one as visible-but-missed, which is the right reading. Closed here: the backup deploy moved to step 6b, BEFORE the 7d callers that write player_create_commands receipts — deploying it at 7f meant a receipt could be created while the old hard-coded backup was still live and silently uncaptured; the runbook named the wrong pending entry for backup_export_group (it is entry 6, 20261118100000, U1c-p4/#646, not 11); backup-database was missing from the §9 rollback manifest, which is now present with its production version marked UNKNOWN for the owner to record at preflight, since it cannot be read from the repository; the post-seed ACL guard is now version-aware, deriving privilege names from acldefault('r', relowner) instead of a list that ended at TRIGGER and therefore missed PostgreSQL 17's MAINTAIN; that guard and the test now also read column ACLs, because has_table_privilege cannot see GRANT UPDATE (state, last_error_code) and that grant alone is enough to drive the state machine; and the named DEFAULT_DENY set is now checked for equality against the deny-list parsed out of supabase/seed.sql, so neither can be retired without the other. The overflow finding was triaged as a documentation defect rather than a code one — 2^63 is not reachable — and the affected 'cannot overflow' sentences were corrected instead, with the test rewritten from a type assertion to a behavioural probe past the int4 boundary.

Owner wording audit of 9f8293316, applied here: the 'UUIDs, states, codes and timestamps' enumerations omitted the self_service boolean and the attempt counter and are now either complete or reduced to 'no direct identifiers'; and the claim that the JSON export otherwise carries no direct identifiers was false — profiles, persons, guest_players, trainer_profiles, invoices and notification_contacts all do, because a restore needs them. The account_deletion_audit exclusion is a data-minimisation decision about one table, not a property of the snapshot.

A later round fixed two test-hygiene defects and deliberately did NOT change this digest, because it changed no migration: the column-grant mutation test re-implemented the ACL question inline instead of re-running the shipped one, so it proved the blind spot existed without proving the assertion closed it; and three trigger-disable sequences had no guaranteed cleanup, so a throw between DISABLE and ENABLE would have left every later test in the file running with no guard. The ACL one is closed by sharing one query (scripts/db/acl-deny-query.mjs); the trigger one by a withTriggersDisabled() helper and an afterEach that fails if any test leaves the trigger off. Verified by mutation: removing the helper's finally makes 25 tests fail with that message — and 15 others still PASS, which is precisely the silent green the guard now prevents.

MANDATORY MCP REVIEW, round 3, thread 019ff127-0ce5-76c2-aa65-29f47a3505b7 (gpt-5.6-sol, ultra, read-only), against 395ae2074: no P1/P2, five P3, all five confirmed and closed here. Round 3 was itself a retry: the first attempt timed out after 1800s with no response, which under this repo's rules means no review occurred, and a CLI fallback was stopped unfinished and never counted.

What round 3 found. ONE was a real test-architecture defect and the same class this suite had just fixed once: the ACL deny query existed twice — in backup-coverage.mjs and copied into the PGlite suite — so deleting the column-ACL branch from the SHIPPED guard left the mutation test green on its own copy while backup coverage stayed green because the reset schema has no column grants. The query now lives once, in scripts/db/acl-deny-query.mjs, imported by both; mutating it now fails the test, verified. The other four were documentation defects, and each was a claim the code did not support: zero-policy RLS was called a deny-all backstop when service_role carries BYPASSRLS and is stopped only by the REVOKE; the lease_expires_at comment said a superseded holder 'can no longer write' when the shipped test proves the opposite; the DATABASE OWNS TIME rule said every caller timestamp is discarded when database_scrubbed_at and finished_at are in fact REFUSED by the immutability check; and the forward-compensation manifest dropped the table without dropping account_scrub_operations_guard(), which DROP TABLE leaves behind.

MANDATORY MCP REVIEW, round 4, same thread 019ff127, against 767341c1d: no P1/P2, four P3, all four confirmed and closed. Two were introduced by the round-3 fixes and two were visible-but-missed. The instructive one: the round-3 test meant to demonstrate that service_role BYPASSRLS defeats a zero-policy table asserted only that count(*) returned a number — which a role WITHOUT bypass also produces, as 0, since RLS filters rather than errors. It now compares against a non-zero owner count and asserts current_user, RLS on and zero policies; verified by mutation, removing BYPASSRLS from the fixture role now fails it. Also closed: 'The fencing window' survived on the lease interval after the fencing claim was retracted elsewhere; and the forward compensation omitted restoring the backup_export_tables() COMMENT (CREATE OR REPLACE preserves it) and regenerating types.ts, either of which would leave the compensated database describing a table that no longer exists.

MANDATORY MCP REVIEW, round 5, same thread 019ff127, against ea3dac754: no P1/P2, one P3, introduced by the round-4 fix and confirmed. Round 5's fix touched no migration, so the digest did not move from the one pinned at ea3dac754. It had moved for round 4: that correction edited migration 20's fencing comment, taking the chain from 69c7d63f (pinned at 767341c1d) to 83ebad7a. Codex also answered the convergence question directly and agreed with the assessment offered to it: the executable state machine has been stable since round 2, and the recurring family is TEST FIDELITY — invariant tests not building their own discriminating fixture. Three rounds, three disguises: round 3 tested a copied ACL rule, round 4 asserted count(*) returned a number (which a non-bypass role also satisfies, as 0), round 5's replacement measured rows other tests happened to leave behind and failed when run alone. Rather than fix the third instance only, the whole file was run under --sequence.shuffle, which found TWO further order-dependent tests Codex had not reported: the legacy-row snapshot (a later test inserts legacy rows) and the inertness count (later tests create operations). All preservation claims are now measured in beforeAll either side of applying the migration and compared capture-to-capture, the BYPASSRLS test builds and rolls back its own sentinel, and the rule is written into the file header. Five shuffled runs pass.

MANDATORY MCP REVIEW, rounds 6 through 9, same thread 019ff127: no P1/P2 in any round, and no executable defect. Every finding was a documentation defect, and most were in text written to explain tests that were already correct. Round 7 named the family — meta-documentation universalising details that deliberately have exceptions — and rounds 8 and 9 confirmed the fix was less text, not better text. The historical and mechanism paragraphs were therefore deleted rather than rewritten again, and what remains points the reader at the queries and the shuffle probe instead of summarising them. The state machine has been unchanged since round 2 and re-verified clean in rounds 3 through 9.

MANDATORY MCP REVIEW, rounds 10 and 11, same thread 019ff127. Round 11 was asked whether anything should block a reviewer, and answered no. Corrections were attempted for the accompanying items, but the closure claim made here at the time was WRONG and is corrected: the stale keyset-paging description was removed only from backup-coverage.mjs's header and the migration, and survived in supabase/functions/backup-database/index.ts, in backup-coverage.mjs's own PAGINATION PRECONDITION block and its two failure messages, and in two places in the B1 test; the 'ever un-erasable' absolute was removed from the migration and the test but survived in the runbook. All of those were fixed later, in the ABC-20 correction pass recorded below. The lesson is the one this file keeps relearning: a claim edited where a reviewer pointed is not the same as a claim removed.

REVIEW STATUS — NOT A CLEARANCE. Rounds 1-2 ran in Codex thread 019ff061-9be2-7ef3-b0ee-720df894d26b. Rounds 3-12 ran in a different thread, 019ff127-0ce5-76c2-aa65-29f47a3505b7. Round 5 exhausted the normal review budget. Rounds 6-12 proceeded WITHOUT prior owner approval and are informational only. Round 12 reviewed d4e984320de364422d50f52d05675dc52e10a37f, which is not the current head, and it was asked a BLOCKER-ONLY question — is there anything a reviewer should block on — rather than the normal threshold of every actionable P1-P3 finding; its answer is scoped to that narrower question and to that SHA, and is not a clearance of it or of any later state. Nothing in this file records or implies clearance of any head. Final clearance is recorded externally, in the coordinator ledger, and never through a further post-review commit to this repository.

ABC-20 CORRECTION PASS — owner-approved, and NOT a review round. Its input was a set of observations read out of an orphaned Codex session file that finished after the ABC-19 MCP client call had already timed out and returned nothing. That call remains NO REVIEW under AGENTS.md; the orphan output is informational evidence only, was independently verified item by item against the code before anything was changed, and is not recorded here as review feedback. No clearance is claimed for any SHA. Substantive changes in this pass: the fencing contract the later RPCs owe now requires a server-minted token AND the monotonic external_attempt_count as a generation term, because lease_token is caller-supplied and can recur, which is ABA; supabase/seed.sql joined both path filters in .github/workflows/migrations.yml, since the post-seed ACL property depends on it and no filter matched it; and scripts/db/u2-scrub-claim-race.mjs was added, racing two real Postgres sessions through claim and reclaim to prove the transition layer serialises — the RPC-level identity fence remains the later slice's to prove. Test fidelity: the in-place lease-extension probe was reaching the wrong guard and now forces the specific refusal; reclaim now proves a database-owned future deadline and that the reclaimed holder can immediately act; the database-owns-time tests gained past sentinels and clock bracketing, without which a LEAST(caller, now) clamp passed; the legacy-untouched projection now covers relacl, owner, RLS, policies and the guard function's prosecdef/proconfig/proacl, and the legacy write contract is driven as service_role, which is what the real writer is; and an adversarial grant to an unnamed role now exercises the generic aclexplode(relacl) branch that no test reached. Documentation corrections are listed in the commit.

ABC-21 MECHANICAL CI/TEST-EVIDENCE CORRECTION — owner-approved, not a review round, no clearance claimed. The migration change is comment-only (the ABA fence contract, stated twice more where it was still written as token-alone), which is why this digest moved. The substantive gap it closes is that scripts/db/u2-scrub-claim-race.mjs was reachable by CI's path filters but had no run: step, so it executed nowhere: it is now an unweakened step in migrations.yml and pinned by name in scripts/ci/workflow-contract.mjs REAL_PG_SUITES, along with the migrations.yml trigger paths. Verified by mutation: deleting the step, adding continue-on-error, or dropping supabase/seed.sql from the pull_request filter each fails the contract. The race harness was also made failure-safe — every guard-disable window is opened and closed inside ONE transaction, rows are recorded at INSERT, and an outer finally rolls back all three sessions, deletes this run's rows and closes every client. Proven, not asserted: a fault injected at four stages (including one raised while the guard is disabled) leaves the trigger enabled, no rows behind and no session open; and while the window is held open a concurrent session samples the trigger 70 times and never once sees it disabled, where the non-transactional version is seen disabled in 36 of 71 samples.

why_the_sanitized_clone_stays_outbound_i: THE ACTUAL PROOF, and it is simpler than the stub-execution story an earlier draft of this record told: on a sanitized rehearsal target the migration never runs past its first statement. Its opening guard is `IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_extension WHERE extname = 'pg_cron') THEN RETURN`, and sql/platform_stub.sql deliberately creates the cron/net SCHEMAS and functions WITHOUT registering a pg_extension row for pg_cron (it only checks that the real extension is absent). So the DO block raises a notice and returns before it reads Vault, before it takes the advisory lock, before it looks up any job, and before cron.schedule is ever called. Nothing is stored and nothing is scheduled.

Because it returns there, the net.http_post text inside the $cmd$ literal is never even written to cron.job on a clone. Even if it were, that call sits inside a string: applying a migration stores such a command, it does not execute it.

Belt and braces beneath that: the sanitizer neutralises CREATE EXTENSION pg_cron/pg_net so the real extensions are never installed, and there is therefore no scheduler process on a rehearsal target to tick a stored command at all.
And beneath that again: the stub's own cron.schedule INSERTs with active = false and its cron.alter_job hard-codes active = false, so even a migration that tried to arm a job could not.

NOT relied upon, and corrected here because an earlier draft of this record claimed it: the stub's cron.job.jobname is GLOBALLY unique, not unique per (jobname, username) as real pg_cron is. This migration's owner-scoped lookup is therefore not exercised on a sanitized target and no claim about it should rest on one. That property is proven instead by src/test/identityCronInert.realpg.test.ts, whose stub models the real (jobname, username) uniqueness.
